```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}

library(tidyverse)

```

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Getting books from Project Gutenberg: 

earnest <- gutenberg_download(844, mirror = "http://mirror.csclub.uwaterloo.ca/gutenberg/")

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#putting books into one word per row format

dorian_words <- dorian |>

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Loading in other data sets for analysis: Stop words and Sentiment analysis (afinn)

smart_stopwords <- get_stopwords(source = "smart")

afinn <-get_sentiments(lexicon = "afinn")


```

# Introduction

"The Picture of Dorian Gray" and "The Importance of Being Earnest" are both brilliant pieces of literature. "The Picture of Dorian Gray" is a dark examination of beauty, youth, influence, and morality as it plays on a Faustian bargain, while "The Importance of Being Earnest" is a comedic play, satirizing morality and marriage with unmatched wit. The most surprising connection between these works that span genre and theme is authorship. Oscar Wilde wrote both of these works in 1891 and 1895, respectively. With the control of a shared author, in this analysis we will explore how analyzing the frequency and sentiment of text can shed light on the differences between these works.

To give a bit of context, here is a brief summary of both works. "The Picture of Dorian Gray" focuses on its titular character, Dorian Gray, a beautiful but naive young man, Basil Hallward, a dedicated painter, and Lord Henry, a hedonistic wit. The novel begins with Basil giving Dorian a portrait of himself and Lord Henry musing on the fragility of beauty and youth. This frightens Dorian, who then wishes that instead of growing old himself, his portrait would grow old instead, exclaiming, "I would give my soul for that!" (Chapter 2). The course of the novel then follows Dorain as he, incresingly influenced by Lord Henry and falling out with Basil, goes around society and builds a reckless reputation. Dorain gets engaged to the young actress Sybil, then abruptly breaks off the engagement after her acting deteriorates. Dorian is harsh to her, and when he returns home, he realizes his cruelty is reflected in the portrait that has developed a sneer. This reveals that Dorian's wish has come true, his portrait takes his ugliness. Dorian wishes to make up with Sibyl, but Lord Henry tells him Sibyl has killed herself. The story then jumps ahead 18 years, where Dorian has accrued a cruel reputation but maintains social standing due to his persistent beauty and youth. Basil comes to confront Dorian, and Dorian reveals what has become of Basil's portrait in the course of 18 years. The painting is horrific, marred with all the age and cruelty of Dorian's past. Basil is horrified, and Dorian proceeds to kill Basil. Dorian faces an increasingly difficult life, tormented by guilt and people he has wronged. In a fit of rage, he stabs the painting, but his servants instead find Dorian dead, finally as an old man, and the painting reverted to its original youthful state.

"The Importance of Being Earnest" primarily focuses on friends Jack Worthing and Algernon Moncrieff. Jack primarily lives in he country, but pretends to have a troublesome brother Ernest in London he needs to check on, so he has an excuse to travel to London often Everyone in London knows Jack only as Earnest, including Algernon and his cousin Gwendolen. Jack proposes to Gwendolen, and she mentions how important it is that she marry someone named Ernest. Lady Bracknell, Gwendolen's mother and Algernon's aunt, enters, and as a matriarch focused on social acceptability, he questions Jack's background. She is dismayed to find Jack was abandoned as a baby in a handbag and doesn't know his parents, birth name, or have any social connections. Subsequently Lady Bracknell refulses to consent to his marriage to Cecily. Meanwhile, Jack has mentioned to Algernon that he has a ward named Cecily who lives in the country, and Algernon decides to meet her while posing as Jack's pretend brother Ernest. They fall in love and get engaged, and Cecily also comments how important it is that she marry someone named Ernest. So both Jack and Algernon run off to attempt to get renamed Ernest, and meanwhile Gwendolen meets Cecily, and they discover they both believe they are engaged to Ernest. Jack and Algernon explain their intent to change their names, and then Lady Bracknell reappears. They are at a stalemate, as Jack will not let Algernon marry Cecily so long as Lady Bracknell stops Jack from marrying Gwendolen, but Lady Bracknell's apprehensions are overcome when it is revealed that Jack is actually Lady Bracknell's long-lost nephew and brother to Algernon, actually named Ernest. Both couples get together, as Jack exclaims that he now knows "the vital Importance of Being Earnest."

# Word Frequency and Theme

The differences in these two works, in style, medium, and theme, can be seen by examining the most common words used in each work. The graph below shows the top 15 words used in each work. Comparing proportions as opposed to absolute counts allows us to compare the works against each other, despite "The Picture of Dorian Gray" being almost four times longer than "The Importance of Being Earnest". Stop words, words that are extremely common with broad purposes such as "the" and "a", are excluded as defined by the smart stop words lexicon.

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Calculating how often each word is used as a proportion of total words

earnest_words_freq <- earnest_words |>
  group_by(word) |>
  summarize(num_word_earnest = n()) |>
  mutate(freq_word_earnest = num_word_earnest / sum(num_word_earnest))

dorian_words_freq <- dorian_words |>
  group_by(word) |>
  summarize(num_word_dorian = n()) |>
  mutate(freq_word_dorian = num_word_dorian / sum(num_word_dorian))

#Put both books into one tibble

books_freq <- earnest_words_freq |>
  full_join(dorian_words_freq) |>
  select( -num_word_earnest, -num_word_dorian) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(freq_word_earnest, freq_word_dorian), names_to = "book", values_to = "freq") |>
  mutate(book = str_remove(book, "freq_word_"), #str_function no. 1
                                                #regex no. 1
         book = ifelse(book == "dorian", "The Picture of Dorian Gray", 
                       "The Importance of Being Earnest"))


```

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Bar plots of top 15 words in each book with and without stop words
#Text Analysis Method no. 1 Word counts/frequencies


#Vector of lowercase character names

books_characters <- c("dorian", "henry", "gray", "harry", "basil", "jack", "algernon", "cecily", "gwendolen", "lady", "bracknell", "prism", "ernest", "chasuble", "worthing", "lane", "bunbury", "merriman", "miss", "cardew")



#Vector to manually choose colors

name_colors <- c("Name" = "thistle4", "Not a Name" = "thistle")


#Bar plot, top 15 words in each work: 

books_freq |>
  anti_join(smart_stopwords) |> #Exclude stop words
  filter(word != "NA") |>
  mutate(is_name = ifelse(word %in% books_characters, "Name", "Not a Name")) |>
  group_by(book) |>
  slice_max(freq, n = 15) |> #Get top 15 words
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(word, freq), y = freq, fill = is_name)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    facet_wrap(vars(book), scales = "free_y") +
    theme_light() +
    labs(title = "Top 15 Words in Each Work", 
       x = "Word", 
       y = "Frequency of Word", 
       fill = "Is the word a name?") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = name_colors) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)

```

In this graph, differences in the structure of each text are pronounced. In the script for a play, a character's name is fully printed before every line of dialogue and in stage directions. In short, character names are used constantly. As a result, the top 4 words in "The Importance of Being Earnest" are all character names as referred to in stage directions. The theme of names in general may also contribute to 11 out of the top 15 words being names, including the name Ernest that does not refer to an actual character. Although "Dorian" is still the top word for "The Picture of Dorian Gray", ultimately only 5 names make the top 15 list. In contrast to "The Importance of Being Earnest," which has many characters and an emphasis on names, "The Picture of Dorian Gray" has a clear protagonist and is more insular to Dorian's sole narrative. We only deeply investigate the life of Dorian Gray and his closest friends, and as a result have far fewer names with far less frequency.

To more accurately compare how themes are reflected in the most frequent words, we shall now look at the same graph, but with names excluded:

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Bar plots of top 15 words in each book with and without stop words or names



#Vector to manually choose colors: 

books_colors <- c("The Picture of Dorian Gray" = "tomato3", "The Importance of Being Earnest" = "lightblue3")



#Bar plot of Top 15 Words in each work, w/out names: 

books_freq |>
  anti_join(smart_stopwords) |>
  filter(word != "NA") |>
  mutate(is_name = ifelse(word %in% books_characters, "Name", "Not a Name")) |>
  filter(is_name == "Not a Name") |>
  group_by(book) |>
  slice_max(freq, n = 15) |>
  ggplot() +
    facet_wrap(vars(book), scales = "free_y") +
    geom_col(aes(x = fct_reorder(word, freq), y = freq, fill = book)) +
    coord_flip() +
    theme_light() +
    labs(title = "Top 15 Words in Each Work (Excluding Names)", 
       x = "word", 
       y = "Frequency of Word") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = books_colors)+
    guides(fill = "none") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```

In "The Importance of Being Earnest", we can see that despite removing names, there is still a decided focus on people. The words "mr", "brother", "aunt", and "sir" reflect the play's focus on relationships and class, as these titles reveal how characters know and address each other. In "The Picture of Dorian Gray," we can see the focus on the portrait itself. Some top words include "time", "eyes", and "face", all of which are wrapped in Dorian's examination of his changing portrait, as he reflects on the passage of time and the cruel twisting of his physical features. The Gothic edge of this novel also comes through in words such as "lord", "love", and "night".

However, despite these novels' differences, we do see strong overlap in the top words, with "don't", "life", "good", "man", "time", "people" and "back" making it onto both lists. Both of these novels were written by Wilde, so we cannot discern if this is reflective of a wider trend in English texts, or if these are unique frequencies to Wilde's writing. We can, however, explore a difference in themes by directly comparing words associated with each text's major themes.

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Bar chart of difference in frequency of theme words: 



#Vector to manually choose colors

books_colors <- c("The Picture of Dorian Gray" = "tomato3", "The Importance of Being Earnest" = "lightblue3")



#Plot word frequency for themes

books_freq |>
  mutate(theme = ifelse(word %in% c("love", "loves", "loved"), 
                        "Both", 
                    ifelse(word %in% c("name", "named", "names", "marry", "married", "marriage"), 
                           "Earnest Themes", 
                          ifelse(word %in% c("beauty", "beautiful", "youth", "young"), 
                                 "Dorian Themes", 
                                    "no")))) |>
  filter(theme != "no") |>
  mutate(theme = as_factor(theme)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = word, 
             y = freq, 
             fill = book)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~factor(theme, c("Dorian Themes", "Earnest Themes", "Both")), 
             scale = "free_x") +
  theme_light() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = books_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Words Divided by Theme", 
       y = "Frequency of Word", 
       fill = "Book")



```

For this graph, I have focused on the themes of beauty and youth for "The Picture of Dorian Gray", marriage and names for "The Importance of Being Earnest", and "love" as a theme in both works. We can see that, in general, when a word is associated with a certain work's theme, that work features the word more often. One exception is the word "young", which features more in "The Importance of Being Earnest" than in "The Picture of Dorian Gray". This discrepancy represents subtler points of theme in both works. "The Picture of Dorian Gray" often refers to youth as a possessive feature Dorian holds, as opposed to the adjective "young". Youth is often personified, as the novel grapples with the implications of youth even aside from a character being young (as the second half of the novel deals with a late 30-year-old Dorian, who despite not being young still praised for his youth). For example, when Lord Henry describes Dorian for the first time, he thinks, "All the candour of youth was there, as well as all youth’s passionate purity." "The Importance of Being Earnest" often plays on Victorian societal expectations for people, which vary according to age. As a result, characters being called "young" is often done to contextualize the rules that apply to characters and to add emphasis to their actions. For example, Jack asks Algernon in Act One, "Why cucumber sandwiches? Why such reckless extravagance in one so young?", which plays on the strictness and expectations placed upon people even in topics as trivial as snacks.

# Sentiment and Story Arc

"The Picture of Dorian Gray" is a fascinating character study, as we watch Dorian go from a relative newcomer on social scenes, rise to it with new experiences, slowly fall as Dorian becomes increasingly careless, and ultimately descend into a miserable life as he cuts out friends and faces consequences of past mistakes. We see this character charm the world, fall out of favor with it, and ultimately crumble after a challenging life. Each of these turns is described in beautiful prose, following all of Dorian's feelings of love, pleasure, guilt, and fear. As a result, sentiment analysis of each word in the novel provides an insightful mirror into the events of the novel itself. The following graphic was created by giving each word a sentiment value as assigned by the "Afinn" sentiment lexicon, where each word is rated on a scale from -5 to 5, with -5 being the most negative words and 5 being the most positive. The novel is then divided into sections of 80 lines each, and the sum of the Afinn value of each word in a section is calculated. The annotations were made as I tried to independently think of the most important plot developments in the novel, and then went back into the text and left markers on the graph for their place.


```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "This graph is an annotated bar chart overlaid with a smoothing line. The x axis represents the sections of the novel, with each section being 80 lines long, and the y axis represents the sum of the sections' afinn value. The x axis ranges from section 0 to section 110, and the y axis ranges from negative 60 to positive 80. The chart also features vertical lines labeled with plot points, including points where Dorian offers his soul in section 11, Dorian gets engaged in section 28, Dorian breaks his engagement and sees his portrait change in section 42, Dorian kills Basil in section 71, and Dorian dies in section 105. We see an increase in the sum of affin sentiment up until Dorian is engaged, and then the sentiment starts to decrease, hitting 0 after Dorian's portrait changes. We see a decline when Dorian kills Basil, and then a leveling off into the end of the novel. In general, we see an expected association between plot points and their sentiment value, for example, after Dorian gets engaged, there is a period of very positive afinn sums, but after Dorian kills Basil, there is a stretch of negative afinn sums."}
#Show sentiment change over course of story with plot point annotations
#Text Analysis Method no. 2 Afinn Sentiment Analysis
#Alt text included in this graph


dorian_words |>
  inner_join(afinn) |>
  mutate(paragraph = linenumber %/% 80 ) |>
  group_by(paragraph) |>
  summarize(sum_value = sum(value)) |>
  
  ggplot(aes(x = paragraph, y = sum_value)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, fill = "tomato3") +
    geom_smooth(se= F, color = "black") + 
  
    annotate("segment", x = 11, y = -65, yend = 80, linewidth = 1, color = "black", alpha = .2) + 
    annotate("text", x = 11, y =60 , label = "Dorian Offers Soul")+
    annotate("segment", x = 28, y = -65, yend = 80, linewidth = 1, color = "black", alpha = .2) +  
    annotate("text", x = 28, y = 70 , label = "Dorian Engaged")+
    annotate("segment", x = 42, y = -65, yend = 80, linewidth = 1, color = "black", alpha = .2) +  
    annotate("text", x = 50, y = 60 , label = "Dorian breaks engagement")+
    annotate("text", x = 50.5, y = 53, label = "and portrait changes")+
    annotate("segment", x = 71, y = -65, yend = 80, linewidth = 1, color = "black", alpha = .2) + 
    annotate("text", x = 71, y = -55 , label = "Dorian kills Basil")+
    annotate("segment", x = 105, y = -65, yend = 80, linewidth = 1, color = "black", alpha = .2) + 
    annotate("text", x = 105, y = -55 , label = "Dorian dies")+
  
    labs(title = "The Picture of Dorian Gray", 
       x = "Section of Novel (each section 80 lines)", 
       y = "Sum of Section's Afinn Value") +
    theme_light()



# Guide for annotations: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/annotate.html

```

The emotion of the words used very well represents the overall arc of the story, as the summary shows the rise and subsequent increasing unhappiness of Dorian Gray. The specific events of the novel also match very well with the summed Affin sentiment values, we see a section of high sentiment around Dorian's engagement, where he poetically professes his love for Sibyl Vane and speaks highly of her and her abilities. We conversely see a patch of negative sentiment over the scene where Dorian shows Basil what has become of the painting, sees Basil's horror, and ultimately kills Basil.

We can create a plot using the same method for "The Importance of Being Earnest":

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Sentiment over time

earnest_words |>
  inner_join(afinn) |>
  filter(word != "miss") |>
  mutate(paragraph = linenumber %/% 80 ) |>
  group_by(paragraph) |>
  summarize(sum_value = sum(value)) |>
  
  ggplot(aes(x = paragraph, y = sum_value)) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, fill = "lightblue3") +
    geom_smooth(se= F, color = "black")+
  labs(title = "The Importance of Being Earnest", 
       x = "Section of Play (each section 80 lines)", 
       y = "Sum of Section's Afinn Value")+
  theme_light()

```

This graph accurately shows the generally positive sentiment throughout the play, the play does have tension and motion, but is generally funny and relatively light-hearted. However, the arc of the novel is less clear from this analysis.

Both novels have beautiful arcs, filled with building tensions, surprising twists, expertly crafted climaxes, and amazing conclusions. And yet the arc is far better represented in the graph for "The Picture of Dorian Gray" as opposed to "The Importance of Being Earnest". There are several reasons for this. A primary reason is the difference in how language is used in each novel. "The Picture of Dorian Gray" is full of prose that highlights the emotions of scenes, and while artistic, it is also honest about characters' perceived emotions. In contrast, "The Importance of Being Earnest" is sarcastic and witty, with characters often saying things they do no mean, and employing words with bazaar sentiments to add to the comedy of the scene. A clear example of this is when Algernon meets Cecily. This scene is light-hearted, romantic, and fun. But looking at the literal text makes this less clear, they joke about Algernon being Jack's "wicked" and "reckless" brother (Scene Two), both of which have negative connotations, which couldn't be further from the teasing nature of the scene itself. Another reason may have to do with the structure of scenes. "The Picture of Dorian Gray" primarily follows one character and has one primary plot. "The Importance of Being Earnest" follows several characters with several unrelated plot points. So, there may be a serious scene that is followed by a more comic one, and the sums cancel each other out to give a less clear direction of the story.

# Word Frequencies Between Characters

Sentiment analysis fits well with "The Picture of Dorian Gray", but the format of a play offers unique analysis opportunities. While "The Picture of Dorian Gray" has dialogue from many characters, thoughts from characters, and observations from an omniscient narrator all mixed together, the play "The Importance of Being Earnest" has a fixed number of characters, with each line attributed to one. As a result, we can easily compare tendencies in dialogue between characters.

These graphics compare the vocabulary tendencies of Jack to Algernon and Jack to Lady Bracknell. The y-axis represents the proportion of time Jack used a given word, and on the x-axis is the proportion of time Algernon or Lady Bracknell use a word. The line y = x is overlaid on each graph to represent when characters use a word an equal proportion of time. Each point represents a word used by the characters, and the points are overlaid with a selection of the words they represent (not all words could be included for the readability of the plot).

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Some data tidying to get each word assinged to the character that speaks it: 

#Put play into a single string: 

earnest_book <- str_flatten(earnest$text, " ") #str_function no. 2
                                               #regex no. 2



#Divide play into a series of strings, each with format "CHARACTER. What their line is"

lines <- str_split_1(earnest_book, "(?=(JACK\\.|ALGERNON\\.|CHASUBLE\\.|MERRIMAN\\.|LANE\\.|LADY BRACKNELL\\.|GWENDOLEN\\.|CECILY\\.|MISS PRISM\\.))" ) #str_function no. 3
                                                       #regex no. 3

#str_split_1 splits the string at points of matches to regular expression
#The ?= in front of the regular expression tells R to keep regular expression in final string pieces
#Source for ?= info: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/74292177/split-a-string-and-keep-delimiter



#Create a tibble

name_line <- as_tibble(lines) |>
  mutate(character = str_extract(value, "JACK\\.|ALGERNON\\.|CHASUBLE\\.|MERRIMAN\\.|LANE\\.|LADY BRACKNELL\\.|GWENDOLEN\\.|CECILY\\.|MISS PRISM\\."),                
         #new column with name of character saying the line
         #str_function no. 4
         #regex no. 4
         line = str_remove(value, "JACK\\.|ALGERNON\\.|CHASUBLE\\.|MERRIMAN\\.|LANE\\.|LADY BRACKNELL\\.|GWENDOLEN\\.|CECILY\\.|MISS PRISM\\.")) |> 
          #remove the name of character saying line from the line
  select(character, line) |>
  filter(!is.na(character)) |>
  mutate(line = str_remove_all(line, "\\[.+\\]")) |> #To get rid of stage directions
                                                     #regex no. 5
  unnest_tokens(word, line) |>
  count(word, character) |> 
  group_by(character) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = character, values_from = prop) |>
  select(word, `JACK.`, `ALGERNON.`, `LADY BRACKNELL.`) |>
  pivot_longer(`ALGERNON.`:`LADY BRACKNELL.`, names_to = "character", values_to = "prop")

```

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
#Plot character word frequencies scatterplot

name_line |>
  anti_join(smart_stopwords) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prop, y = `JACK.`)) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0.0065, y = 0, yend = .0065,
  colour = "gray") +
  geom_point(alpha = .7, position = position_jitter(), size = 2, color = "lightblue3") +
  geom_text(aes(label = word), position = position_jitter(), check_overlap = T)+
  labs(title = "Comparative Frequency of Jack and Algernon Word Use", 
       x = "Frequency Algernon/Lady Bracknell Used Given Word", 
       y = "Frequency Jack Used Given Word") +
  theme_light() +
  facet_wrap(vars(character))



#This code inspired by our textbook, https://www.tidytextmining.com/tidytext


```

Jack and Algernon are approximately the same age and close friends, while Lady Bracknell is Algernon's aunt and acts as a matriarch and pillar of victorian standards. Despite these differences, the distribution in the two graphs is very similar, with most words clustering around the y = x line, scattered outliers above the line representing a variety of words used more often by Jack than Algernon or Lady Bracknell, and fewer words below the line.

Some interesting points include the name "Ernest" being almost exactly the same amount by both Algernon and Jack, who both pose as Ernest throught the novel. We can also see who the characters are closest to, as Jack says his partner's name, Gwendolen, more than Algernon or Lady Bracknell, and Algernon uses his partner's name, "Cecily," more often than Jack. We can also see Algernon's obsession with Bunbury.

# Conclusion

Despite having the same author, it is not a super surprising result that there are major differences in the words used in "The Importance of Being Earnest" and "The Picture of Dorian Gray". One is a comedic play, the other a Gothic novel, and while both renound peices of literature, they are divergent in atmosphere, message, and medium. But it is surprising how well text analysis is able to pick out these differences. In picking out word frequencies, we can see the high proportion of names featured in the script of a play, the thematic leanings of each work, and how character frequencies show their interactions with plot. In performing sentiment analysis, we can see the arc of the story and make conjectures about the work's structure. Text analysis provides a unique insight and offers methods of structured anlayis to learn about these literary masterpieces. 


ach graphic is able to help shine light on differences in theme, genre, and structure in a really unique way.
